kept.subject: Purshia tridentata
kept.rationale: In a southeastern Oregon post-fire planting trial at a site whose long-term precipitation (283mm/yr) and elevation closely match the Boise pilot envelope, antelope bitterbrush seedling mortality was almost total (496 of 500 died by year two) even after exotic annual grass competition was chemically reduced, because first-growing-season drought overwhelmed any competitive release; this indicates high near-term establishment risk for bare-root/direct-seeded bitterbrush plantings under Boise-comparable precipitation without irrigation or a wetter planting year.

source.title: Reducing Exotic Annual Grass Competition Did Not Improve Shrub Restoration Success during a Drought
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: Imazapic herbicide successfully cut exotic annual grass cover and raised native bunchgrass cover, but only 4 of 500 planted bitterbrush seedlings survived to the second year, with first-year drought identified as the overriding mortality driver.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.1016/j.rama.2022.08.001 resolves to Davies, Bates & Svejcar (2022), Rangeland Ecology & Management, exact title match. Full text confirms: 500 bitterbrush seedlings planted across 5 SE Oregon sites (2014 Buzzard Fire Complex), elevation 1,310-1,460 m, long-term MAP 283 mm (matching the condition envelope exactly), only 4 of 500 survived to year two, and imazapic reduced exotic grass cover but did not improve bitterbrush establishment because first-year drought was the overriding mortality driver. Outcome 'unfit' and rationale are fully supported by the source, not overstated.

kept.subject: Pinus ponderosa
kept.rationale: Across three New Mexico ponderosa pine seed sources in the 524-672mm/2,239-2,950m semi-arid montane band, seedlings grown under low nursery irrigation (55% container water-holding capacity) were smaller at time of outplanting but showed higher net photosynthesis, better water-use efficiency, and more hydraulically active xylem when transplanted into simulated drought — meaning bare survival/establishment for restoration plantings is achievable but contingent on deliberate moisture-limited nursery conditioning rather than standard well-watered nursery culture.

source.title: Physiological and morphological responses of Pinus ponderosa seedlings to moisture limitations in the nursery and their implications for restoration
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: Low-irrigation nursery conditioning produced smaller ponderosa pine seedlings but increased net photosynthetic rate, water-use efficiency, and hydraulically active xylem, improving simulated outplanting drought performance relative to well-watered nursery stock.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.3389/fpls.2023.1127656 resolves to the exact-title Frontiers in Plant Science 2023 article. Confirmed via full-text table: three NM seed sources (Manzano 524 mm/2,239 m; Philadelphia Canyon 672 mm/2,319 m; Valle Vidal 591 mm/2,950 m) exactly bracket the claimed 524-672 mm / 2,239-2,950 m envelope. Low-irrigation (55% WHC) nursery conditioning produced smaller but more drought-resilient seedlings (higher photosynthesis, WUE, hydraulic function) under simulated outplanting drought, matching the supporting quote. 'Marginal' outcome is a fair, hedged characterization (contingent on deliberate nursery conditioning) rather than an overstatement, since the study is nursery/simulated-drought based, not field survival data.

kept.subject: Cercocarpus ledifolius
kept.rationale: In a two-summer northeastern Utah/Great Basin field experiment, curl-leaf mountain mahogany first-year seedling survival depended jointly on water supplementation, herbivory protection, and microhabitat: survival was highest beneath mature C. ledifolius canopies and rose sharply with added water and herbivore exclusion during the dry (27.7mm summer-precipitation) year, indicating the species is restoration-viable in this region but establishment is fragile without facilitative microsites, supplemental water, or browse protection in dry years.

source.title: Positive and negative interactions between environmental conditions affecting Cercocarpus ledifolius seedling survival
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: Water supplementation and herbivory protection during a dry summer (27.7mm precipitation) generally increased first-year seedling survival, with survival tending to be greatest beneath mature C. ledifolius canopies rather than in open interspaces.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.1007/s004420100757 resolves to Ibáñez & Schupp (2001), Oecologia, exact title match. Confirmed: two-summer (1996-1997) Utah/Great Basin experiment crossing water supplementation, herbivory protection, and three microhabitats (open, under Artemisia, under mature C. ledifolius); during the dry 1996 summer (27.7 mm precipitation, matching the quote) water and herbivore protection increased survival, and survival tended to be greatest beneath mature C. ledifolius canopies -- matching the rationale's microhabitat claim precisely. 'Marginal' outcome (viable but fragile establishment) is well supported.

kept.subject: Pinus monophylla
kept.rationale: Along a 2,100-2,450m elevation gradient in the semiarid Shoshone Mountains, Nevada, singleleaf pinyon establishment depended strongly on Artemisia tridentata nurse-shrub microsites: shrub cover let seedlings overcome an early establishment bottleneck and facilitation was strongly positive at the seedling/early-juvenile stage but shifted toward neutral once trees transitioned to adult foliage, and this facilitation dependence held across the elevation gradient rather than only at the driest sites — implying pinyon restoration succeeds best when paired with existing or planted sagebrush cover rather than bare interspace seeding.

source.title: Shrub facilitation of tree establishment varies with ontogenetic stage across environmental gradients
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: Artemisia tridentata shrub microsites allowed Pinus monophylla to overcome an early population bottleneck and establish in areas without existing tree cover, with the net facilitation effect shifting from strongly positive to neutral as trees transitioned from juvenile to adult foliage.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.1111/nph.15957 resolves to Urza, Weisberg, Chambers & Sullivan (2019), New Phytologist, exact title match. Confirmed: field study of Artemisia tridentata / Pinus monophylla facilitation in the Shoshone Mountains, Nevada, across an elevational gradient; net facilitation shifted from strongly positive to neutral as pinyon transitioned from juvenile to adult foliage, and interaction outcomes were not strongly related to elevation -- matching the claim that facilitation dependence 'held across the elevation gradient rather than only at the driest sites.' The specific 2,100-2,450 m elevation figure was not independently pinned down but is plausible for the described pinyon-juniper woodland site and not contradicted by anything found.

kept.subject: Populus fremontii
kept.rationale: Across eight Fremont cottonwood populations spanning a 5.3C mean-annual-temperature gradient in the hyper-arid lower Colorado River Basin, trees rely on transpirational (evaporative) leaf cooling to stay within a lethal thermal safety margin; recent heatwaves have exceeded even this species' unusually high heat-tolerance threshold, and cottonwood forests have declined rapidly in the last decade where temperatures exceed roughly 50C — meaning the species is restoration-viable only where sustained groundwater or surface-water access supports the transpiration needed for leaf cooling, not as a rain-fed planting in a semi-arid setting.

source.title: Limits of thermal and hydrological tolerance in a foundation tree species (Populus fremontii) in the desert southwestern United States
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: Despite an exceptionally high critical temperature for photosystem II function, recent heatwaves in the lower Colorado River Basin have exceeded that threshold, forcing P. fremontii to rely on evaporative leaf cooling to maintain thermal safety margins, and cottonwood forests have declined rapidly where temperatures exceed roughly 50C.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.1111/nph.19247 resolves to Moran et al. (2023), New Phytologist, exact title match ('Limits of thermal and hydrological tolerance in a foundation tree species (Populus fremontii) in the desert southwestern United States'). Confirmed: eight P. fremontii populations across a 5.3C MAT gradient in the lower Colorado River Basin rely on evaporative leaf cooling to stay within thermal safety margins; despite an exceptionally high Tcrit, recent heatwaves have exceeded it, and P. fremontii forests have rapidly declined over the last decade in places where temperatures sometimes exceed 50C -- matching the supporting quote almost verbatim. 'Marginal' outcome (restoration-viable only with sustained water access for transpirational cooling) is a fair, non-overstated reading tied to reduced Colorado River flows being flagged as a critical threat in the abstract.

kept.subject: Robinia pseudoacacia
kept.rationale: The species' native-range optimum of 1,020-1,830mm annual precipitation is roughly three to six times the Boise pilot's 280-400mm envelope; even the reduced 500-550mm threshold at which introduced European populations remain drought-tolerant still exceeds Boise's precipitation supply, and the same review notes low adaptive capacity to arid conditions produces stunted, dwarfed growth outside its moisture range — indicating black locust is a poor rain-fed fit for this semi-arid intermountain setting and would require supplemental irrigation to avoid stress-stunted growth, separate from its documented invasive/riparian nitrogen-cycling concerns.

source.title: Biological Flora of the British Isles: Robinia pseudoacacia
source.supporting_quote_or_finding: R. pseudoacacia grows best in its native range under 1,020-1,830mm annual precipitation, and although drought-tolerant introduced populations persist down to 500-550mm, the species shows low adaptive capacity to arid conditions, resulting in stunted growth and dwarfism.

citation_check.reason: DOI 10.1111/1365-2745.12162 resolves to Cierjacks et al. (2013), Journal of Ecology, exact title match ('Biological Flora of the British Isles: Robinia pseudoacacia'). Confirmed: native-range optimum growth at 1,020-1,830 mm annual precipitation (matching the condition envelope exactly), drought-tolerant introduced European populations persisting down to 500-550 mm, and low adaptive capacity to arid conditions producing stunted growth and dwarfism -- matching the supporting quote closely. 'Unfit' outcome for the ~280-400mm Boise envelope (well below even the 500-550mm drought-tolerant threshold) is a sound, conservative inference, not an overstatement.

kept.subject: Camelina sativa
kept.rationale: In an 8-year field trial at the WSU Lind Dryland Research Station (crop-year precipitation averaging 281 mm, range 193-375 mm; Ritzville silt loam), replacing one fallow year of a 2-year winter wheat-fallow rotation with spring camelina produced a harvestable oilseed crop (avg. 643 kg/ha seed yield) but left a soil-water deficit that persisted through the following 13-month fallow period and reduced subsequent winter wheat yield relative to the standard wheat-fallow rotation. Camelina is agronomically viable as a fallow-replacement crop in this precipitation zone but carries a real water-carryover cost to the cash wheat crop, matching the low end of the Boise-pilot precipitation envelope closely.

source.title: Soil Water Dynamics with Spring Camelina in a Three-Year Rotation in Washington's Winter Wheat-Fallow Region
source.journal: Soil Science Society of America Journal

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to Wuest & Schillinger, SSSAJ 2019, title matches exactly. Abstract (Semantic Scholar) confirms an 8-year study finding that 'extending the crop rotation to include camelina was costly in terms of water use, surface soil residue cover, soil water storage during the fallow, and WW grain yield' — matches the claimed 'marginal' outcome (viable oilseed crop but real water-carryover cost to subsequent wheat). Lind, WA / Ritzville silt loam / ~280mm precipitation zone is consistent with the claimed envelope.

kept.subject: Vicia villosa
kept.rationale: At the USDA-ARS Central Great Plains Research Station near Akron, CO (421 mm mean annual precipitation, 1384 m elevation, silt loam soils, semi-arid continental climate), hairy vetch grown as a spring green-fallow legume replacing part of the fallow period decreased available soil water at winter wheat planting and depressed subsequent winter wheat grain yield compared with conventional bare fallow. In a single-fallow-replacement, water-limited winter wheat system like the Boise pilot, this soil-water drawdown makes hairy vetch a poor standalone fit despite its strong nitrogen contribution.

source.title: Legume Green Fallow Effect on Soil Water Content at Wheat Planting and Wheat Yield

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to Nielsen & Vigil, Agronomy Journal (published 2005, matching the label's stated year despite the '2004' DOI segment), title matches exactly, authors are the Akron CO USDA-ARS station named in the rationale. Verbatim abstract confirms hairy vetch was one of four legumes tested (Austrian winter pea, spring field pea, black lentil, hairy vetch) and explicitly states 'there were no significant differences in available soil water at wheat planting due to legume type' and that legume water cost 'may be too great to justify use of legumes as fallow cover crops... in semiarid environments' — this supports generalizing the negative finding to hairy vetch specifically, since the paper found no species-level difference.

kept.subject: Pisum sativum
kept.rationale: On a long-term organic dryland farm in semiarid northern Montana, winter pea green manure (terminated at pod stage) contributed 14-20 kg N/ha more soil NO3-N than fallow, used 26-31 mm less soil water than comparison pea management treatments, and increased the following organic winter wheat's grain yield by 13-39% and protein by 1.5 percentage points. This is an in-region, positive result for winter pea as a nitrogen-building, comparatively water-conservative legume option in a semi-arid intermountain wheat rotation, contrasting with hairy vetch's negative water/yield tradeoff in a similar system.

source.title: Pea green manure management affects organic winter wheat yield and quality in semiarid Montana

kept.subject: xTriticosecale
kept.rationale: In a 7-year dryland no-till corn-millet-triticale forage sequence at Akron, CO (421 mm MAP, 1384 m elevation, silt loam, semi-arid), winter triticale produced the greatest average forage dry matter (5367 kg/ha) of the three crops and had the highest probability of exceeding 4000 kg/ha dry matter, with dry matter production tightly linked to water use, indicating strong water-use efficiency for forage production under low-precipitation dryland conditions.

The specific yield figures (5367 kg/ha, >4000 kg/ha probability) are plausible full-text results not visible in the abstract but not contradicted by it.

kept.subject: cover_crops
kept.rationale: A global meta-analysis of 137 studies across 76 sites and 15 countries, stratified by precipitation class including a <400 mm dryland band matching the Boise pilot envelope, found that cover cropping (versus bare fallow) decreased soil water storage at winter wheat planting by 16.3%, decreased wheat yield by 7.0%, and decreased water-use efficiency by 26.3% in winter wheat monoculture systems. This is a negative finding specifically for cover crops as a water-and-yield-preserving fallow substitute in dry, single-crop winter wheat rotations, cautioning against blanket cover-crop adoption in the driest part of the target precipitation range without complementary practices (e.g., no-till/residue retention, which the same meta-analysis found improved outcomes).

The paper also confirms a <400 mm precipitation stratification class matching the label's condition envelope (0-400 mm).

kept.subject: agroforestry
kept.rationale: Field-shelter (windbreak) effect on spring wheat in the Northern Great Plains was strongly dependent on soil water status: beneficial when irrigation removed the water constraint, but detrimental under dryland (rainfed) conditions where the shelterbelt/crop competed for limited soil water. This is a direct caution for windbreak agroforestry in a water-limited semi-arid cropping context like the Boise pilot area, where most cropland is not irrigated at the field margin.

kept.subject: agroforestry
kept.rationale: Synthesizing many field studies, this review shows windbreak/shelterbelt yield response is spatially bimodal - a loss zone immediately leeward and a larger gain zone further out - and that the percentage yield benefit scales with regional/annual dryness, i.e. windbreaks are not a uniformly positive intervention but one whose net effect on yield depends on where in the field you measure and how dry the site is.

kept.subject: silvopasture
kept.rationale: In a semi-arid Mediterranean holm-oak dehesa (a classic silvopasture system), isolated trees did not strongly draw down near-surface soil water used by understory forage during the growing season because they relied on deep water reserves instead - but that deep-water uptake extended across the whole inter-tree space and continued depleting through summer, so the system reduces (rather than eliminates) tree-forage water competition, at the cost of deep soil-moisture drawdown.

source.title: Wildfires and climate change push low-elevation forests across a critical climate threshold for tree regeneration
source.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: Regeneration exhibited a threshold response to annual climate (VPD, soil moisture, max surface temperature); dry sites across the study region crossed these thresholds over the past 20 years, and high fire severity plus low seed availability further reduced regeneration probability.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves (via PNAS) to Davis et al. 2019, PNAS, title matches verbatim: 'Wildfires and climate change push low-elevation forests across a critical climate threshold for tree regeneration.' Abstract and independent corroboration confirm '33 wildfires' across 'four regions across the western United States' (matching the label's '33 wildfires and four western US regions'), the nonlinear threshold response to VPD/soil moisture/max surface temperature, and that dry sites crossed thresholds over the past 20 years with high severity fire and low seed availability further reducing regeneration. Condition envelope and outcome ('mixed' — divergent outcomes inside vs outside the climatic envelope) accurately reflect the source; nothing is overstated.

kept.subject: reforestation
kept.rationale: A western-US-wide post-fire reforestation planning tool, built from regeneration probability and planted-seedling survival models across all 11 western states, finds hydroclimate is the dominant gate on outcomes: planting pays off on climatically suitable sites but shows reduced survival and is a poor investment on warm, dry sites such as the Southwest and arid parts of the southern Rockies. This argues for climate-based site screening before committing planting budget in a semi-arid pilot area rather than treating reforestation as uniformly effective.

source.title: A post-fire reforestation assessment and prioritization tool for the Western United States

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: Hydroclimate is strongly tied to regeneration success, with reduced survival of planted trees in warm, dry areas like the Southwest and arid sites within the southern Rocky Mountains.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves (via Springer/Fire Ecology) to the 2025 Regenmapper paper, title matches verbatim: 'A post-fire reforestation assessment and prioritization tool for the Western United States.' Full text (PMC) contains the supporting quote nearly verbatim: 'hydroclimate is strongly tied to regeneration success, with reduced survival of planted trees in warm, dry areas like the Southwest ... and on arid sites within the southern Rocky Mountains.' Caveat: the rationale overstates the tool's construction, claiming it is 'built from regeneration probability and planted-seedling survival models' — the paper explicitly states Regenmapper models only natural regeneration probability (not planted-seedling survival) and the planted-survival claim is attributed to other cited studies (Ouzts 2015; Rodman 2024; Marshall 2024) rather than being this paper's own finding. This is a meaningful but non-disqualifying embellishment given the core quote/outcome are accurately sourced and the confidence was already flagged low; recommend downstream reviewers discount the 'planted-seedling survival models' framing specifically.

kept.subject: reforestation
kept.rationale: Following a high-severity fire in northern New Mexico, survival of planted ponderosa pine, pinyon, southwestern white pine, and Douglas-fir seedlings depended heavily on which post-fire shrub sheltered them: survival was 10-35 percentage points higher under Gambel oak than under New Mexico locust because its denser canopy buffered temperature, humidity, and vapor pressure deficit. This shows planting outcomes in the dry interior West are conditional on microsite facilitation choices, not a uniform treatment effect.

source.title: Post-fire early successional vegetation buffers surface microclimate and increases survival of planted conifer seedlings in the Southwestern United States

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: Seedlings planted under Gambel oak had survival rates 10% to 35% greater than those planted under New Mexico locust, driven by lower temperature, higher humidity, and lower vapor pressure deficit beneath the denser shrub canopy.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves (via Canadian Science Publishing) to Crockett & Hurteau, title matches (trivial capitalization difference: 'Southwestern' vs 'southwestern'). Journal matches (Canadian Journal of Forest Research). Content match is exact and strong: independent sources confirm the 10-35% survival advantage under Gambel oak vs New Mexico locust, driven by lower temperature/higher humidity/lower VPD, in northern New Mexico post-fire plantings — matching the supporting quote precisely. CAVEAT: the claimed publication year (2021) is incorrect; CrossRef and independent search confirm the article was formally published in 2022 (Vol. 52, Issue 3, pp. 416-425); '2021' likely reflects the DOI's embedded manuscript-year token, not the actual publication year. This is a citation metadata error that should be corrected (year -> 2022) but does not point to a different/wrong work — the DOI unambiguously resolves to the exact paper described, with all substantive findings verified.

kept.subject: managed_grazing
kept.rationale: Global meta-analysis (235 sites, 18 countries) found controlled/rotational grazing at high stocking density was the only grazing strategy that significantly raised topsoil soil organic carbon stocks and content versus continuous free grazing; in the paper's own arid-to-semi-arid climate class (MAP 300-550mm) the gain was smaller than under moist-humid conditions but still a significant, positive, quantified increase, supporting managed/rotational grazing as a viable soil-carbon strategy for Boise-analog semi-arid rangeland, with the caveat that the semi-arid effect size is the weakest of the climate classes tested.

source.title: On the impact of grassland management on soil carbon stocks: a worldwide meta-analysis

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: Controlled grazing with high density of grazers (CHG) significantly enhanced soil organic carbon stocks (effect size 0.477, +5.9% yr-1 on average), and under the paper's arid-to-semi-arid climate class specifically the increase was +15.6 g C m-3 yr-1 (1.9% yr-1), a smaller but still positive gain compared to +233 g C m-3 yr-1 (8.9% yr-1) under moist-humid conditions.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves via Crossref/OpenAlex to the exact title 'On the impact of grassland management on soil carbon stocks: a worldwide meta-analysis', Geoderma Regional, 2021/2022 (Phukubye et al.). Retrieved abstract summary confirms 235 sites/18 countries, controlled high-density grazing (CHG) as the standout positive practice, and explicit statement that effectiveness 'varied by climate zone', which supports the label's arid/semi-arid vs moist-humid breakdown. Full text was paywalled/bot-blocked, so the precise numeric effect sizes cited (0.477 effect size; 15.6 vs 233 g C m-3 yr-1) could not be independently confirmed, but nothing retrieved contradicts them and the qualitative claim (smaller but still positive semi-arid effect) is consistent with what is verifiable. Outcome label 'effective' is a fair reading of the paper's own policy recommendation to adopt CHG grazing.

kept.subject: managed_grazing
kept.rationale: A ranch-scale, multi-year field comparison at the USDA Central Plains Experimental Range shortgrass steppe (Colorado, semi-arid, 320mm MAP, 1650m elevation) found that adaptively managed multipaddock rotational grazing produced vegetation/forage outcomes statistically indistinguishable from season-long continuous grazing at the same stocking rate, while continuous grazing achieved greater cattle weight gains -- i.e., rotational grazing did not outperform simple continuous grazing on either forage or livestock-production metrics in this semi-arid shortgrass system.

source.title: Adaptive, Multipaddock Rotational Grazing Management: A Ranch-Scale Assessment of Effects on Vegetation and Livestock Performance in Semiarid Rangeland

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: When adaptive multipaddock rotational management was directly compared with continuous grazing at the same increased stocking rate, continuous grazing achieved similar vegetation outcomes but with greater cattle weight gains than the rotational system.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to the exact title 'Adaptive, Multipaddock Rotational Grazing Management: A Ranch-Scale Assessment of Effects on Vegetation and Livestock Performance in Semiarid Rangeland', Rangeland Ecology & Management, 2020 (Augustine, Derner et al.). Retrieved abstract states rotational grazing caused a '12-16% reduction in total cattle weight gain relative to continuous grazing' and 'minimal benefits for perennial grass density or production' -- directly matching the label's supporting quote and rationale. Study site/authors (Augustine, Derner -- USDA-ARS Central Plains Experimental Range researchers) are consistent with the claimed Colorado shortgrass steppe location and condition envelope. 'Mixed' outcome is a defensible characterization (similar vegetation, worse livestock outcome).

kept.subject: managed_grazing
kept.rationale: In semi-arid Borana rangeland (Ethiopia), managed grazing exclosures (a deferment/rotational strategy) roughly doubled soil organic carbon and total nitrogen relative to continuous open grazing at sites with low woody encroachment, but the benefit disappeared (statistically insignificant) at heavily encroached sites -- showing the strategy's soil-carbon benefit is conditional on rangeland vegetation state, not a universal effect. Out-of-region evidence, kept as a low-confidence global data point illustrating a genuine mixed/negative-condition finding rather than a cherry-picked positive.

source.title: Managing Semi-Arid Rangelands for Carbon Storage: Grazing and Woody Encroachment Effects on Soil Carbon and Nitrogen

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: At low woody-encroachment sites on sandy clay soils, grazing exclosures showed roughly twice the soil organic carbon and total nitrogen of open-grazed sites, but at heavily encroached sites on sandy loam soils the difference between exclosure and open grazing was not statistically significant.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to the exact title 'Managing Semi-Arid Rangelands for Carbon Storage: Grazing and Woody Encroachment Effects on Soil Carbon and Nitrogen', PLOS ONE, 2015 (Yusuf, Treydte, Sauerborn). The publisher's own landing page abstract contains a near-verbatim match to the label's supporting quote: soil OC/TSN unchanged under exclusion at heavily encroached sites but roughly double at low-encroachment sites. Minor flaw: the condition_envelope's soil_texture (sandy_loam, clay_loam) doesn't precisely match the rationale's own text ('sandy clay soils' at low-encroachment sites) -- an internal imprecision, not a refutation-level mismatch. Label is appropriately flagged low-confidence and out-of-region, which is honest self-disclosure rather than misrepresentation.

kept.subject: biochar
kept.rationale: A 5-year field trial at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's High Plains Agricultural Laboratory near Sidney, NE (western Great Plains, semi-arid, ~457mm MAP, silt loam) found wood biochar needed a fairly high application rate (at least 6.25 Mg/ha) to raise crop yield at all, the benefit was inconsistent year to year, and the soil-property gains were concentrated in fertility (nutrient) measures rather than physical/water-holding properties, with benefits fading between year 1 and year 5 -- a marginal, rate- and time-dependent outcome rather than a clear win.

source.title: How does biochar impact soils and crops in a semi-arid environment? A 5-yr assessment

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: At least 6.25 Mg biochar ha-1 was needed to improve some soil properties and crop yields in this semi-arid silt loam, biochar improved soil fertility properties more than physical properties (including water-related properties), and the soil/yield benefits were greater in year 1 than by years 3 and 5 of the trial.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to the exact title 'How does biochar impact soils and crops in a semi-arid environment? A 5-yr assessment', Field Crops Research, 2024, vol. 310 (Blanco-Canqui, Creech, Easterly). kept.subject: biochar
kept.rationale: A 3-year, 4-site, 10 site-year irrigated field trial across Utah (Cedar City, Cornish, Elberta, Mosida -- directly adjacent to the Boise pilot's Intermountain West/BSk climate zone) tested wood biochar on alfalfa, corn, and wheat and found essentially no reliable benefit to yield, crop quality, or plant-available soil water/water tension across sites and years; wheat yield actually declined slightly as biochar rate increased, leading the authors to explicitly conclude the amendment was not effective for boosting production or conserving irrigation water under arid agriculture.

source.title: Biochar had minor effects on yield, quality, and water availability of irrigated alfalfa, corn, and wheat

kept.supporting_quote_or_finding: Across 10 site-years in Utah, incorporated biochar increased silage corn yield by 12% in one year but decreased it 10% the next, topdressed biochar had no effect on alfalfa yield in any year, and wheat grain yield declined by about 0.01 Mg/ha for every additional 1 Mg/ha of biochar applied, with no consistent effect on soil water tension -- leading the authors to conclude this wood biochar was not an effective tool for crop production or water conservation in arid agriculture.

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to the exact title 'Biochar had minor effects on yield, quality, and water availability of irrigated alfalfa, corn, and wheat', Agronomy Journal, 2022 (Holt, Yost, Winward, Creech, Allen, McAvoy). Crossref returned the full abstract, which matches the label almost verbatim: two Utah studies at two sites each, 2018-2020, irrigated alfalfa/corn/wheat, silage corn +12% in 2018 then -10% in 2019, wheat yield declining 0.01 Mg/ha per 1 Mg/ha biochar applied, 10 site-years total, and the explicit conclusion that biochar 'was not an effective tool for enhancing short-term crop production or conserving irrigation water in arid agriculture'. Author affiliation with Southern Utah University (Cedar City) confirms one of the named sites. Strongest-verified label of the set; outcome 'ineffective' is directly supported.

rejected.subject: Panicum miliaceum
rejected.rationale: In the same Akron, CO dryland no-till sequence (421 mm MAP, silt loam, semi-arid), proso millet had the steepest water-use-efficiency regression slope of the three crops tested (33.0 kg ha-1 mm-1 vs. 24.2 for corn), showing it converts scarce water into biomass efficiently, but its average forage dry matter (3283 kg/ha) was well below winter triticale's (5367 kg/ha), making it a workable but lower-ceiling dryland forage option relative to triticale in the same low-precipitation system.

source.title: Fallow replacement cover crops in a semi-arid High Plains cropping system

citation_check.reason: DOI resolves to Holman, Obour & Assefa, Crop Science 2021, title matches exactly, location (Garden City, KS) matches. However the verbatim abstract states 'Spring triticale had up to 182% more forage accumulation over other forage cover crops and a 108% grain yield advantage over other grain cover crops' — i.e., triticale, not sorghum/sudangrass, was the standout performer. The label's claim that 'sorghum/sudangrass was the most productive of the grass-type cover crops evaluated (ranking above cereal rye, triticale, wheat, oat, and barley)' directly contradicts the actual reported result and also conflates Sorghum bicolor's role as the rotation's main cash crop (the 'S' in the WSF wheat-sorghum-fallow rotation) with being one of the tested fallow-replacement cover crops.
